newsitem.title: USA: Motorola earnings fall in quarter.
newsitem.headline: Motorola earnings fall in quarter.

text.p: Motorola Inc. said Thursday earnings fell 45 percent in the fourth quarter, hurt by previously announced restructuring charges, but that the cost-cutting would pave the way for higher earnings.

The maker of cellular phones, computer chips and other electronic gear said net income fell to $238 million in the quarter, from $432 million in the 1995 quarter. Sales grew 5 percent to $7.69 billion from $7.30 billion.
Earnings per share fell to 39 cents from 72 cents. The earnings were slightly below the 41 cents a share that Wall Street analysts had expected, according to First Call, which tracks estimates.
For the year, Motorola said it earned $1.15 billion, down from $1.78 billion as sales grew to $28.0 billion from $27.0 billion. Earnings per share fell to $1.90 from $2.93.
Motorola said earnings were reduced by $150 million in the quarter from restructuring and other one-time charges. The various charges had been announced last year.
It said its semiconductor business lost money in the quarter, though sales and orders for the key products grew in the quarter from the third quarter.
Motorola stock rose 62.5 cents to $64 on the New York Stock Exchange in regular trading, before the company released its results. In after-hours trading, the shares rose to $65.
The Schaumburg, Ill.-based company said cost-cutting and other actions taken in the fourth quarter were taken to spark a rebound in earnings growth in 1997.

"We have initiated a reinvigorated process of discontinuing those development programs that have not lived up to their promise, further reducing costs in existing businesses that are not achieving adequate profitability, and refocusing our investments," Chief Executive Officer Christopher Galvin said in a statement.

Motorola also said it has begun to see increases in orders and sales as the semiconductor industry starts to rebound, though improved year-over-year financial results may not be evident until later in 1997.
Sales of semiconductor products accounted for 29 percent of Motorola's 1995 sales.
